newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel to restart passenger trains.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel to restart passenger trains.

text.p: Passenger train services will resume through the fire-damaged Anglo-French Channel tunnel on Wednesday, tunnel operator Eurotunnel said on Tuesday.

Eurostar, which runs the express passenger trains between London and Paris and Brussels, said it would resume 90 percent of its normal services on Wednesday. A spokesman said it would run 13 trains per day to Paris and seven to Brussels.
Debt-laden Eurotunnel will restart its Le Shuttle passenger vehicle services from December 10.
The tunnel has been closed to all passenger traffic since November 18, when a fire on a truck destroyed a freight shuttle train and severely damaged a section of the tunnel, injuring 34 people.

The decision followed news that the Inter-Governmental Commission (IGC) of French and British government representatives had accepted the advice of its safety committee that a limited service could resume while repairs continued.

Eddie Ryder, the head of the British delegation for the Channel Tunnel Safety Authority, which advised the IGC, told reporters: "It (the authority) is now satisfied that the necessary safety equipment is available and that revised operating and emergency procedures are in place."
However, Ryder said the freight vehicle shuttles could only resume after the completion of a French investigation into the causes of the fire, which started on such a vehicle.
Ryder said that it was limiting the resumed services to six trains per hour. A Eurotunnel spokeswoman said normal traffic was around nine trains an hour, including the freight shuttles.
Eurotunnel staged a drill on Sunday to prove that it could safely run passenger services when one of the two rail tunnels is still closed for repairs.
Eurotunnel, which has been struggling to reach agreement with its banks to restructure nine billion pounds ($15 billion) of debts, was clearly relieved that services were poised to begin again.
"We are absolutely delighted," said a spokeswoman. "This is an early Christmas present for Eurostar and the shuttle tourist customers."

Eurostar has also been working hard to boost traffic this year since its British arm was sold by the government to the London and Continental Railways (L&CR) consortium in return for taking on a three-billion-pound ($2 billion) project to build a new fast rail link between London and the tunnel.

Eurostar, which is a joint venture between Eurostar UK and the French and Belgian national railways, said it was running up to 24 return services a day from London to Paris and Brussels before the fire.

Eurostar said last month that demand had increased from a rate of 3.9 million to 6.4 million passengers a year in the 12 months to end-August following the introduction of a range of special fare offers and other promotions earlier this year.
But L&CR has said it needs to boost traffic to over 10 million passengers a year to help fund the building of the fast rail link.

L&CR's partners included bus transport firm National Express, British entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group, investment bank SBC Warburg, U.S. project management specialist Bechtel and civil engineering consultants Over Arup and Halcrow.
